extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy of science; scientists interested in foundations and methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Statements and canons about the legitimate limits and methods of scientific inference: when to infer entities (e.g., consciousness), what counts as scientific knowledge (sense-impressions/sensation), and how to judge traditions, beliefs, and identity. Includes illustrative examples and warnings about illegitimate extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference of consciousness requires observable machinery and interval
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is an interval between sense-impression and exertion (filled with stored sense-impressions and conceptions) and similar 'machinery' can be observed, we may infer consciousness (and associated will). In lower forms of life, a shorter interval and reduced intensity may justify inferring reduced consciousness. We have no right to infer consciousness where we can find no interval between sense-impression and exertion or where we can find no nervous system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/anti-patterns: It is illogical to infer consciousness in matter or in postulated immaterial existences where no nervous system or interval can be found; ejecting will/consciousness into such matter is 'enormously exceeding' scientific inference and forms inconsistent conceptions (centaur-like). Footnote: 'Consciousness without a nervous system is like a man without a vertebral column — a chimera.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon i — No belief where reason cannot be applied
rubrics_metrics.description: Where it is impossible to apply man's reason, that is to criticise and investigate at all, there it is not only unprofitable but anti-social to believe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Belief should be an adjunct to knowledge and a guide to action where probabilities are weighed but decision is needful. Belief in spheres where we cannot reason prejudices action in spheres where we can reason. (Example: irrational faith that harms social action.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern meaning of belief — credit on balancing probabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief now denotes credit given to a statement on a more or less sufficient balancing of probabilities, rather than absolute certainty based on external authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This marks transition from uncritical faith to weighed probability; treat belief as fallible credit used for action when full knowledge is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon 2 — Infer only from like to like in similar surroundings
rubrics_metrics.description: We may infer what we cannot verify by direct sense-impression only when the inference is from known things to unknown things of the like nature in similar surroundings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-examples: may not infer an 'infinite' consciousness outside physical surroundings of finite consciousness; may not infer a man on the moon simply because of likeness to ourselves when surroundings differ materially. The environment/setting must be sufficiently similar for a legitimate inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon 3 — Conditions for accepting tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: We may infer the truth of tradition when its contents are of like character and continuous with men's present experience, and when there is reasonable ground for supposing its source to lie in persons knowing the facts and reporting what they knew.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The tradition that Wellington and Blücher won Waterloo fulfils conditions; the miracle of Charlemagne and the adder does not. Emphasises continuity with present experience and credible source proximity to facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon 4 — Different standards for rapid minor decisions vs. permanent conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: It is reasonable in minor actions where rapidity is important to infer on slight evidence and believe on small balances of probability; but it is opposed to society's true interests to take as a permanent standard of conduct a belief based on inadequate testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance as habitual guides to conduct of beliefs based on insufficient evidence leads to erosion of individual responsibility for important decisions. Example: one has no right to believe at 7:00 that a cab will be on the stand at 8:00 if catching an important train at 8:30 depends on it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science deals with sense-impressions (sensation) as ultimate material
rubrics_metrics.description: Science ultimately deals with conceptions drawn from sense-impressions; its legitimate field is the whole content of the human mind (immediate or stored sense-impressions). The outer world for science is a world of sensations known only as sense-impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological implication: do not treat 'things-in-themselves' as part of scientific knowledge. Science uses phenomena (sense-impressions) to test and verify conceptions; beyond sense-impressions we cannot legitimately assert laws or causal relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: External world is a construct from immediate and stored sense-impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Any group of immediate sense-impressions we project outside ourselves and hold to be part of the external world; together with stored impressions this construct is what we term a phenomenon or 'real' for practical life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: the telephone exchange clerk who only has access to messages — the 'real outside world' for him is the aggregate of his constructs from messages. Implication: our perception of reality is conditioned and limited by our nervous system and organs of sense; similarity of these across humans explains commonality of the 'outside world.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 'outside' and 'inside' depends on immediate sense-impression
rubrics_metrics.description: For an individual, the distinction between the real world and his thought of it is the presence of some immediate sense-impression; what is 'outside' vs 'inside' at any instant depends entirely on the amount of immediate sense-impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the needle's properties (thin, bright, pointed) are sense-impressions projected outward, while pain from pricking is termed 'in ourselves' though both are sense-impressions. The division is practical and arbitrary; limits of the group of sense-impressions we term an individual cannot be scientifically drawn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reality and individuality consist in persistent grouping of sense-impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: The reality of an object or individual's identity consists, for us, in the persistency or sameness of the majority of the group of sense-impressions by which we identify it; individuality is recognised by sameness of great majority of sense-impressions at two instants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: blackboard → table transformations show that 'sameness' of material is not a sound basis for individuality; a friend altered in all sense-impressions would cease to be that friend for us. Thus identity is practical, based on repeated experience and grouping of impressions rather than a shadowy 'thing-in-itself.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid postulating 'things-in-themselves' beyond sense-impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unnecessary and unjustifiable to postulate shadowy unknowables behind groups of sense-impressions to account for permanence or reality; such postulates lie beyond the field of scientific conception and inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphysical speculations (Matter, God, Will, Mind-stuff) do not help explain why sense-impressions remain linked. We can only describe unknowns as having the capacity to produce sense-impressions, but assuming laws or causes beyond experience is unwarranted. Practical rule: restrict scientific claims to what can be part of the mind's contents (phenomena/sensation).
